It further creates additional hardship for the Defence which had already struggled to recover from the Prosecution's lapse in compliance with its disclosure obligations. Thus, a trial adjournment would allow the Defence to return to the state of trial preparedness it would have been in, had the guidance remained unchanged. The Defence lists five issues, which had particularly affected its trial preparations, and they will be addressed below. The Prosecution opposes the motion, arguing that the Defence has mis-characterised the Chamber's clarification and amendment to the guidance, and has not demonstrated that the changes had an impact on its trial preparations, such that would justify a considerable adjournment in the proceedings. It notes that it had not altered its Rule 92 ter package and, thus, the Defence knew what the Prosecution would seek to tender with the next witnesses for at least 30 days before their respective testimony. It further submits that contrary to the Defence's portrayal, the Chamber's guidance did not replace the Tribunal's Rules but rather represents the Chamber's preference in respect of the tendering and presentation of evidence which, in exceptional circumstances, may be modified. The Chamber will examine whether the extent of the allegedly unforeseen latest modifications to the guidance justify the granting of a six-month adjournment in the proceedings or, in the alternative, whether a clear error of reasoning or the need to avoid injustice warrant a reconsideration of the Chamber's additional clarification and amendment of the guidance. The Chamber reiterates that its guidance is meant to provide an indication to the parties of its strong preferences with regard to the tendering and presentation of evidence during trial, with the aim of achieving a streamlined presentation of evidence that is concise and efficient. The Chamber recalls that upon showing of good cause and on a case-by-case basis, leave to depart from the guidance may be granted. Therefore, in view of the nature of the guidance, the Chamber considers that any potential burden on the Defence should primarily be assessed in light of how the guidance is applied in practice. In this respect, the Chamber notes that currently there are Rule 92 bis and quater motions with regard to two witnesses pending before the Chamber, and that Rule 92 ter motions filed by the Prosecution mainly relate to witnesses who will be heard after the summer recess, that is, in at least a month's time. Further, in relation to the Defence's concerns about the last-minute changes to the guidance, the Chamber notes that the guidance, due to its very nature, is subjected to developments and modifications. The Chamber will now address the five issues raised by the Defence in its motion. First, the Defence raises the issue of allowing the Prosecution to tender additional supplementary witness statements or statements on distinct subjects. As to the tendering of additional supplementary statements, this modification was already introduced on the 24th of April, 2012, that is well before the adoption of the additional clarification and amendment. But even taken together with the recent modifications allowing additional statements on distinct subjects, in light of the relatively low number of Rule 92 bis, ter, and quater motions filed so far, the Chamber considers that these amendments do not substantially affect the Defence's trial preparations. Second, the Defence argues that the Prosecution would now be permitted to present an unlimited number of associated exhibits. This is not correct. In accordance with the Tribunal's jurisprudence, the Chamber's additional clarification and amendment to the guidance allows for the tendering of documents pursuant to Rules 92 bis to quater, if they form an inseparable and indispensable part of a witness's testimony. Further, the Chamber allows the parties to tender associated exhibits without the witness commenting on them in court under certain circumstances only, when they do not disturb the clarity of the presentation of witnesses' evidence. This, as explained by the Chamber, would apply to documents of a very specific type. Furthermore, the guidance has not set any limitation on the number of exhibits that can be introduced with Rule 92 ter witnesses, as long as they are presented in court and commented on by the witness. The Chamber therefore considers that the Defence's preparations in this respect have not been substantially affected. Third, the Defence addresses the increase and the Prosecution's examination-in-chief time-limits and the lack of the corresponding increase in the Defence's lengths in cross-examination. As explained in the additional clarification and amendment, the Chamber had already decided on the times for examination-in-chief prior to the 19th of June, 2012. Furthermore, although the additional clarification and amendment to the guidance does not address the time-limits for cross-examination of 92 ter witnesses, the Chamber recalls that in its recent decisions on the Prosecution's 92 ter witnesses, it stated that the exact amount of time available for cross-examination depends on many factors and may also be re-evaluated depending on how the cross-examination is conducted. These relevant factors include, inter alia, the length of the examination-in-chief or whether the witness is called viva voce or pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Fourth, the Defence protests against the use of transcripts from other proceedings before the Tribunal, which in its view has now been allowed. The Chamber recalls that its guidance of the 10th of November, 2011, indicated that transcripts of testimony a witness gave in other cases would only be admitted into evidence in exceptional circumstances. The additional guidance merely clarifies the Chamber's initial view by, inter alia, explaining that while the Chamber will not always insist that a statement be taken from witnesses who have not previously provided any, it will carefully consider the party's reasons before deciding on the admission of transcripts of testimony. Fifth, the Defence claims that the tendering of exhibits during re-examination presents an opportunity for the Prosecution to withhold exhibits, preventing the Defence from addressing them in cross-examination. The Chamber notes that this issue does not, as such, arise from the additional clarification and amendment to the guidance. It will nevertheless address the Defence's concerns. In this respect the Chamber recalls that Rule 85 of the Rules provides the general sequence as to the presentation of evidence and examination of witnesses, which can only be varied in the interests of justice. The Chamber considers that it is inevitable that the Prosecution limit the presentation of its evidence during its examination-in-chief, in the interests of expediency and efficiency. The parties should not flood the Chamber with material during their case in chief, with a view to anticipating and pre-emptively responding to all possible opposing evidence. Should the Prosecution, in accordance with the guidance, introduce evidence during re-examination, the Defence will have an opportunity to address this new evidence in further cross-examination. The Chamber does not consider that this has substantially affected the Defence's preparation for trial so far. In view of the above, the Chamber is of the upon that the additional clarification and amendment of the guidance introduced limited modifications to the Chamber's guidance on the tendering and presentation of evidence, as previously amended on the 24th of April, 2012. Further, the Defence has failed to show that these modifications have indeed impeded on its ability to effectively proceed with the trial to the extent that would justify granting any adjournment in the proceedings. As to the Defence's request for reconsideration, the Chamber considers that the Defence has failed to demonstrate a clear error of reasoning or the risk of injustice that would necessitate a reconsideration of the impugned additional clarification and amendment of the guidance. And the Chamber accordingly denies the motion. And this concludes the Chamber's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you said you hoped that you would be able to finish today your cross-examination. If some time would be left, perhaps limited, I do not know how much time you need, Mr. Elderkin, but for re-examination, of course it's difficult to assess at this very moment, but if we could conclude the testimony of this witness today, let's try to achieve that. Welcome back, Mr. Koster. Mr. Petrusic will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on page 4 and page 4 in both versions of your statement, you said that you met representatives of the civilian authorities twice, and you say that the person involved was probably the mayor and that that occurred probably sometime in mid-May. So I'm referring you to your statement, page 4, paragraph 5 from the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what's the question for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Koster, can you tell us what did the mayor request of you? Did he make any requests or did he merely make some complaints?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: During that visit we spoke about negotiations concerning logistics supplies and their delivery. I don't remember exactly what he asked or whether they were specifically complaints.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly that he did ask you for some supplies?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: We spoke about the negotiations for exchanging supplies for food and other materials, but I -- unfortunately I don't remember the exact negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender into evidence document 1D0073 [as interpreted], please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. That is, Mr. Petrusic -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, we are talking about the questionnaire? No. Mr. Petrusic, what document because -- forgive me for not having always all the numbers by heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the document about --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which spoke about the delivery of food --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the delivery of food, separating food from UNHCR, that was not about delivery of food, but about separating and obtaining. That was the language used in that document. Any objections? Not. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D00073 becomes Exhibit D26, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Petrusic, it would assist the Chamber that if you refer to documents or quote from documents, that you do it very precise and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, when you arrived on the 22nd January 1995, did you find there at the location some other international organisations that were headquartered in Potocari or Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I did meet other international organisations but not on the 22nd.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In other words, after your arrival, that was my question; and you gave me an affirmative answer. Now, did you co-operate with the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you mean UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I recall that we did indeed contact UNHCR on a few occasions after the period of 22nd January 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the UNHCR fuel depot was also situated in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I can't determine the exact location of the fuel depot, but I do know that UNHCR had a fuel depot in the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Petrusic please repeat the question; it was not entirely audible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge whether your battalion often used UNHCR fuel?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I recall that at least once, but perhaps several times - I'm not sure about that part - used UNHCR's fuel in consultation with UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You were acquainted with Lieutenant Rutten, a lieutenant of your battalion. Correct me if I am wrong .

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That appears from the statement, isn't it, Mr. Petrusic? He's mentioned many, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know that he mentioned him, but I would like to hear his answer. Anyway, it's all right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, please next question and then it will appear what the problem may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have document 1D00092.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We are waiting for the document, and in the meantime I'm going to tell you that that's the diary kept by Mr. Rutten as of January until 21st of July, 1995, while he was in Srebrenica. And the part that is relevant for the Defence are pages 53 and 54. I'm talking about the version in English. In English it's the bottom of page 53 and the beginning of page 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And your question is, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question is: Sir, do you see at the beginning of page 54 that it is said by Mr. Rutten that there was enough fuel for the month of May?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I can read that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, bearing in mind all of this, was there enough fuel for your units and your patrols to be able to carry out their mission; in other words, to go on patrols around the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, a time-frame would that -- would you focus on May or would you focus on any other point in time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period from the time when the Dutch Battalion arrived until the end of May 1995, bearing in mind of course the previous document as well.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I can recall in the period you're referring to, the last diesel transport we received in the enclave was on 18 February; and from that point we simply used our reserves and operationally we started to minimise use of motorised transport or at least as far as diesel is concerned. So we applied the stage of minimising diesel use in our operations. I'm not sure whether this is what Lieutenant Rutten is referring to, I can't determine that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the whole of the diary or this portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only pages 53 and 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is there any other portion -- is there any other portion you would like to rely on because you have read literally I think what was in the diary: "There is enough diesel for the month of May." If that's the only quote, I wonder whether we would need -- if there is no dispute about the fact that it was part of Mr. Rutten's diary, whether we need the diary at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no dispute that that quote comes from Major Rutten's diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Petrusic, do you still insist on -- or would you refrain from tendering this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed and put your next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, please take a look at your statement, page 4, the one-but-last paragraph. This is the English version and the fourth paragraph in the Serbian version, the version in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Koster, do you feel comfortable with reading the English version of your statement, where of course you signed the Dutch one? I mean your knowledge of the English language is sufficient to follow the question in English if you read it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. President, if you allow me to address you, perhaps it would be faster if it would suit Mr. Koster to have the English version of his statement in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a hard copy is available, that could be provided to Mr. Koster, preferably a non-annotated version. Meanwhile you put your next question to the witness, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Koster: Whose observation posts are you referring to here?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the DutchBat observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you have prevented in any way this kind of conduct of the members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or members of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I have a question about that. Do you mean me personally or do you mean DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, I do apologise to you for this lack of understanding, but you are right. So was it the Dutch Battalion that could have stopped this kind of thing from happening, such incidents, that is?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I think that enough protests were lodged to the Muslim fighters in that period not to fire at the Serbs. Apparently that did, nonetheless, instigate such incidents despite the protests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to try and intervene here. It does look as if there is miscommunication here. This paragraph you're referring to, Mr. Petrusic, it seems to be saying that the observation posts and patrols sometimes came under fire during this period. You asked the witness whose observation posts these are, and he said they belonged to the ABiH. Now, you can't then ask whether he can stop the ABiH from doing what they are doing because it is -- they are supporting the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Looking at the paragraph you referred the witness to, sir. I'm not looking at the following paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Judge, but my understanding was that during the night Muslim fighters would take up position at the observation posts of the UN, the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did I misunderstand your statement, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: In my statement I indicated that the Muslim fighters did indeed take position at the observation post during the night to fire at the Bosnian Serb side and the observation posts were DutchBat ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Further on you said that you lodged protests with higher commands. Did you try to disarm the members of the Muslim units?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: You're still saying "you," and I wonder whether this is addressed to me personally or is it about DutchBat? And I explained that we spoke with the leadership of the Muslim fighters. I just indicated that we protested and I don't know, or at least I can't recall, whether this was the leadership of the Muslim fighters. So I don't know whether you mean me or DutchBat in your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic and Mr. Koster, if Mr. Petrusic puts a question wherein he wants to refer to you as a person and not DutchBat, then he'll clarify that; otherwise, you can understand "you" to refer to you and DutchBat. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could you please repeat the question one more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we have sufficiently resolved this dilemma regarding the observation posts, so now I would like to move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your statement on page 5, paragraphs 3 and 4 in the English version, and page 4, the penultimate paragraph in the Serbian version, are you referring to the removal of observation post E at the south of the enclave? You do recall that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I can recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After this movement -- actually, can you tell us how long this combat lasted?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After this movement, I mean after the observation post was moved, did the Drina Corps forces intend to move towards the enclave or did they stop once the observation post was changed, as it were?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't know which unit took up observation post Echo. I do know that at that point they didn't get beyond observation post Echo as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So your command, did it have information to the effect that before this observation post was taken Muslim armed forces left and went to the area in front of this observation post, taking away property that belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please can we move on to page 7, paragraph 3 from the top of the page in English, and page 6, paragraph 4, in the Serbian version. This is already the time of the beginning of combat around Srebrenica. Sir, that is what you refer to here. Would you agree with me that the day referred to here is the 9th of July?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I'm referring to early July 1995. I don't recall the exact date, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when soldier Renssen lost his life? He was a member of the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Raviv was indeed a member of DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You don't know the date of his death?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember that date now, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the other members of the Dutch Battalion, were they aware of the fact that Private Renssen had lost his life?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: You mean in that period from what I understand? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, in that period.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, it was indicated. I was in the operations room when that report arrived, and later on it was confirmed to other members of DutchBat that Raviv Renssen did unfortunately die.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the cited paragraph, you say that observation posts U and S were taken and that your colleagues were given the choice of returning to base or to drive into Serb territory, which would mean that they were being taken as prisoners of war. So these two observation posts were taken by members of the Drina Corps who were carrying out operations at the time. Is that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I recall that the observation posts Uniform and Sierra were taken by Bosnian at the time, I just don't know what unit they were taken from -- excuse me, they were taken from Bosnian Serbs at the time, I just don't know what unit they were from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that Private Renssen lost his life in the following way, he was going back from his observation post, he was returning to base in Potocari? He was in an APC.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I know that he was in an APC and was on the way back to the enclave towards Srebrenica and Potocari, and that's where he was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was wounded by members of the Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, what does the statement clearly say in this respect? Ten Muslim fighters said that the armoured vehicle could not go any further, nevertheless they decided to carry on. One of the Muslim fighters threw a hand-grenade -- that's evidence. Why is there any need to repeat that? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, these soldiers from the observation posts U and S that were taken by the Serb forces on the following day, did they surrender to the Army of Republika Srpska? Because they did not dare return because of the threat of retaliation by the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that they opted to fall into the hands of the Bosnian Serb army, and I can't speak on behalf of the choice of Sergeant Bresser and van Eck because I didn't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You were Major Franken's deputy; right?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: In the period that I was logistics lieutenant in the enclave, I was the substitute of Major Franken, and when the combat started I was commander of the quick reaction force instructed by the DutchBat operations room. That was the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that Major Franken had issued this order of opening the encirclement, if you will, so that the Muslim population could come in? Why not simply open the gate so that they could enter?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I received that order from Major Otter. As far as I recall, the decision was to get the Muslim population that was fleeing the most protected route possible to the compound, and the route along the road by the gate was in full view and offered all kinds of opportunities to shoot at the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On that first day in the afternoon, that is to say the 10th of July, did the refugee population arrive in your base?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I recall in the afternoon of July 10th there was not yet a massive flow of refugees outside. We did encounter several people from the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to draw your attention to page 8 of the statement. I think that it's the last paragraph on page 8 and the first paragraph on page 9, the first and second paragraphs on page 9. In the Serbian version it is page 7, paragraphs 2 and 3 from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what's the question for the witness, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, on whose orders did you carry out this mission?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: At the time I was under the command of Major Otter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So on his order?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: On Monday, July 10th, when we went outside and made a hole in the gate and prepared to receive some refugees, I was under his command. I was his group commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the question of Mr. Petrusic was whether he gave you the order to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To go outside the compound and make a hole in the fence, I was instructed by Major Otter to do that and to get my people ready to receive the refugees, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on whose order did you meet with one of the commanders of the Muslim fighters of the northern part of the enclave, Mandzic? Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I remember that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the essence was, what the topic of that meeting was, what the agenda was?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: At the first meeting, we were asked what we were doing there as DutchBat. Later that evening I had a second meeting and the Muslim fighters asked about help and to what extent the UN would intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, is that the same Mandzic from that part of the enclave from which you had been banned, where you were not allowed access?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't know. The man I spoke with during the first meeting was introduced to me as Mandzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, I'm looking at the clock. It's time for a break, but I'd first like to have the witness escorted out of the courtroom. We'll have a break of approximately about 20 minutes, Mr. Koster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, how much time do you think you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To be quite frank, Judge, I need more than the time that is left if I were to do all the things I had planned to do. I have the 11th, I have Potocari, the 11th, 12th, 13th, I'm talking to you about the topics that I have to deal with. Until now I've been told I've used up 75 minutes. I don't know whether that is correct or not, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is not only looking at minutes but also at the way in which the cross-examination is conducted. Let me just confer with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the Chamber has carefully considered the way in which the cross-examination was conducted. I once looked at my screen and saw that for 30 seconds you did not put a question at all to the witness. I had to invite you several times just to put a question to the witness. Apart from that, the relevance and the fact that often matters are obvious or already clearly in the statement. Having considered all that, the Chamber has decided that you have half an hour after the break to conclude your cross-examination. We take a break and we'll resume at five minutes passed 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we're now going to move to page 14, paragraph 4 in English, and page 12, paragraph 2 in B/C/S. In order to be as efficient as possible, I'm going just to quote that you said that the bodies of the victims were usually buried on the northern part. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is the last sentence of that paragraph, just to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I stated at the time, then I stand by that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many bodies were buried at that location?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I cannot remember that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximate number, Mr. Koster? Was it 10? Was it 200? Can you give any indication?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, more likely fewer than 10 than something near 200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you keep any records or lists of the burials?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I remember that DutchBat made a note of the position where several bodies were believed to be buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was the cause of death of the persons buried there and when did the death occur?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you exactly what the cause of the deaths was. I know that the time of death must have been around July 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Must have been or was it indeed?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: As I recall, it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did your command report the burials either to the local authorities or to any of the international organisations?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let's now move to the events of the 13th of July, when you and another fellow officer of yours saw ten dead bodies near your compound, and that's an page 15 of your statement, paragraph 1. Now, tell me first, are you acquainted with Private or officer Dorst [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name of a fellow officer Dorst.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Was he together with you on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No. My fellow officer Dorst was not together with me in the situation as it is described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So these dead male bodies that you found positioned as you described, you don't know if they were Serbs or Muslims, do you?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I wasn't able to determine that at the time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, you put to the witness that on page 15 of his statement that he was referring to ten dead people. In the statement I see only the number of nine persons lying on their bellies with their heads bent forward. Could you clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge. I'm sure I said "nine bodies." It's probably a translation issue. We may listen to the audio recording, but obviously we are talking about the people who are described on this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. That was only for the clarity of the record. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, then you go on to say that they wore civilian clothes. Can you tell me, how did you deduce that the wounds on their backs were 2 centimetres in diameter?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: That was an estimate at the time. I walked among the bodies and at the time examined the bodies close up, so that's how I made that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But, sir, you can only see that visually if you remove the top garment of the victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What was your question, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you agree with me that the only way to see this is if one removes the top garment of the victim and that it's impossible to see how the wound looks like if you don't remove the clothes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrusic, the clear factual question would be: Did you, Mr. Koster, remove or change the position of the clothes of those persons you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The wounds were visible through their clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Then you say that around the bodies you saw pieces of paper, documents of a kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any question or are you just quoting from what the statement already says, Mr. Petrusic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: From these documents, were you able to establish anything about the identity of the individuals lying in that field?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No. Several documents looked like they were official documents. I couldn't read them, but some of them bore stamps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were there any photographs attached to these documents?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And then you went on to say that you threw away these documents at the moment when you saw a soldier in the vicinity; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what the statement says, Mr. Petrusic. Please put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So being afraid of the soldier that you saw, you threw away the documents; right?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No, that's not true. We removed the documents after we had been fired at and were going to return to the position where the Bosnian Serb soldiers were taken away, the refugees, and we thought that a Bosnian Serb soldier had reported on us. And we wanted to be free to issue our report. So that's why we threw the documents away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the evening of the 12th -- 11th and the morning of the 12th, did you have any information about the fact that your commander, Karremans, was holding meetings with General Mladic in Bratunac, as well as with the Muslim civilian population? Do I need to repeat my question? Did you know --

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The first part was inaudible of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware of such meetings being held.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that meetings were being held between Karremans and Mladic, and I remember -- I don't remember that meetings with representatives of the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After the first meeting, did the commander or anyone else from the command tell you that an agreement had been reached for the Muslim population that had already been assembled in Potocari to be transferred to Kladanj?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I know that it was at a certain point agreed that the Muslim would be transferred, but unfortunately I don't remember the region Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This knowledge of yours, that the Muslims were going to be transferred, does it pertain to the period prior to the arrival of the buses?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No. I was aware of this after the period the buses arrived. As far as I recall now, it was after that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In one of the video-clips you identified two, as you say, Serb soldiers named Mane and Mickey respectively. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were they present in the area on both the first and the second days?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: What exactly do you mean by the first and the second day?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Were they present in the area of Potocari inside and outside the compound, or rather, beyond red-and-white tape that you put up after midday 12th of July and after the morning of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I saw the two Serb soldiers I recognised as Mane and Mickey. I met them on the evening of the -- of July 12th. I did not see them on the compound personally to the extent I was there because my duties were outside the compound with the refugees, and I don't recall whether I saw them on July 13th at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. These persons, Mickey and Mane, was he a person of authority, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Whether these were those persons, they were introduced to me as the people who at that time were in charge on behalf of the Bosnian Serb military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who introduced you in that way -- who introduced them to you in that way?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, at this time I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, if I tell you that Mane and Mickey were representatives, or rather, members of the unit called the special brigade of the MUP of Republika Srpska commanded at the time by Ljubisa Borovcanin, would you agree with me that this is a correct statement? Allow me, in accordance with the suggestion my colleague gave me, to clarify that MUP stands for the Ministry of the Interior or the police.

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No. At the time they were introduced to me as the people who were in charge on behalf of the Bosnian Serb military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: All the people who were there - we even saw a frame showing soldiers with K-9s, were all these soldiers uniformly dressed; in other words, did they wear identical uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, some of the uniforms varied. So to answer your question as to whether all the uniforms were identical, that's not how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, were the uniforms worn by Mane and Mickey dominant in comparison with the uniforms worn by other people present?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember that properly. I didn't pay careful attention as to whether all uniforms were about the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you speak about the separation of men, according to your estimate did that include men of military age?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I can remember and based on what I saw, I saw middle-aged men at the white house, I saw young men, and yes, I -- I saw some occasional middle-aged men.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection was there only one house that you have just mentioned where the separated men were put up?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Previous response ended with "men of military age."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether there were multiple houses. All I remember is that the men that I described, I saw them at what I've said was the white house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, General Mladic did not enter the UN compound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a question, Mr. Petrusic, or would you like to hear from the witness whether he saw General Mladic entering the UN compound on the 13th of July? Could you answer that question, Mr. Koster.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: My question was: Did General Mladic enter the UN compound on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I can't remember. I was working primarily outside the compound to protect the refugees, so I don't remember and I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But you do remember that he went in the direction of Srebrenica, in his vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I didn't hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The question was whether you remember that he went in the direction of Srebrenica in his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that he did not get out of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: When he was passing me, I remember that he did not get out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have completed the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. I even see that you did it within the limits the Chamber said. It took less than half an hour we granted to you. Is there any need for -- yes. Before I give an opportunity to Judge Fluegge to put questions to the witness, would you -- is there any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: If I may have a couple of minutes on two points.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On a two points.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll first -- Judge Fluegge will first put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One additional question in relation to Mane and Mickey, what was the colour of their uniforms, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Your Honour, the colour of the uniforms was mainly green. I don't remember clearly whether this was mixed with camouflage green, but the person I described as Mickey was wearing a light blue and light lilac jacket, flak jacket, bullet-proof jacket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, you have an opportunity to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Colonel, at page 59 of today's transcript you were questioned about Muslim fighters taking up positions at night at the observation posts, which were DutchBat observation posts. What did you mean when you said the Muslim fighters took up positions at the observation posts?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: By "position," I mean that they were in the area of the observation post, and from the area of the observation post they fired at the Bosnian Serb side, expecting to instigate return fire from that side, from the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And at page 67 of the transcript, you were asked about whether you knew if the nine bodies you found in civilian dress were Serbs or Muslims. First, was the area where you found those bodies within that of the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. That location was within the Srebrenica enclave that the UNPROFOR DutchBat was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Elderkin, looking at that map, could there be any doubt about it? It was 2- or 300 metres from the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That was to set up the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: I only have a few more on this point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Colonel, did you ever see any males in civilian dress whom you believed to be Bosnian Serbs within the area of the Srebrenica enclave up to and including the 13th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No. As far as I can remember, I did not see any Bosnian Serbs in civilian dress or armed in the enclave. I didn't meet any.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: And did you see any Muslim fighters in Potocari or around the area of the bodies after the time on the night of the 10th of July when you had the meeting with the four ABiH fighters?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: No. At the time I didn't see any Muslim fighters in the area of the location where we found the nine bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you very much, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. ELDERKIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Elderkin. Further Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one question for you triggered by one of the questions by Mr. Elderkin. You said: "As far as I can remember, I did not see any Bosnian Serb in civilian dress or armed in the enclave." If you would see a person just in passing, how would you know whether he's a Serb or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: I can't distinguish them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore if you said I never saw a Serb civilian in the enclave, if I understand your answer now well, that you say I won't know whether I've ever seen any of them because I could not distinguish between civilians being Muslim or Serb?

utterances.speaker: EELCO KOSTER
utterances.text: That's what I meant by that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions triggered by those raised by the Judge? Mr. Petrusic, no further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Koster, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to this courtroom and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I'd like to -- you're excused and you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber thinks it has dealt with all the outstanding procedural matters at this moment, but, Mr. Lukic, you may not agree with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately not, Your Honour. We have to inform you about uploaded videos so if you -- it's actually pages from 65 ter Exhibit 19814, so if you want us to do it in written submission we can inform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know how formal it is. If it is purely practical then --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's purely practical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then an informal communication with Chambers staff would do, of course to be copied to the Prosecution. And we don't have to decide immediately on that at this moment, so then we leave it at that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and it's now on the record that we will receive messages from you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we're still trying to find our way with these videos, apart from sending messages to Chambers staff, both parties are invited to communicate with the representative of the Registry, so as to sort out what has now been uploaded so that Madam Registrar is able to assign numbers to it which -- on which of course we'll then later decide on admission. Anything else? If not, I'd like to thank just now before the summer recess all those who are assisting us in our work, that is, security, translators, transcribers, everyone who plays a role in the smooth continuation of these proceedings, and perhaps for today a special thanks for our guest interpreters. We adjourn and we will resume on Tuesday, the 21st of August, at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom III. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
